message.content: The total number of distinct chess games has been estimated by Claude Shannon in 1950 as roughly 10^120. This figure, known as the Shannon number, represents a lower bound on the number of possible games that can be played from the starting position to the end of the game. It is derived from an estimate of the branching factor (about 35) and the average length of a game (around 80 moves), giving 35^80 ≈ 10^120. In other words, there are on the order of one hundred vigintillion possible ways a chess game could unfold.
